english: local rice dish with hamburger patty, egg, and gravy
missing.usage: A staple Hawaii diner comfort dish composed of a bowl of hot white rice topped with a hamburger patty, a sunny-side-up fried egg, and rich brown gravy.
examples: Ho, I stay starving, we go get one loco moco from da diner.
Two scoop rice and extra gravy on top da loco moco.

english: salted salmon side dish with tomatoes and onions
missing.usage: A classic Hawaiian side dish made with diced salted salmon, ripe crushed tomatoes, sweet Maui onions, and crushed ice.
examples: No forget da lomi salmon for da luau plate.
Lomi salmon taste so ono wit poi and kalua pork.
missing.origin: Hawaiian (lomi = massage or mix by hand)

english: octopus or squid simmered in taro leaves and coconut milk
missing.usage: A cherished traditional Hawaiian stew prepared by slow-cooking tender octopus or squid with young luau (taro) leaves, coconut milk, and sea salt.
examples: My tutu make da best squid luau on da island.
Squid luau stay rich and sweet from da coconut milk.

missing.usage: Seasoned, cured, and salted dried flank steak, traditionally broiled or pan-fried; staple of pupu platters and luau spreads.
examples: Pass da pipikaula, brah, dat beef so ono!
We brought poke and pipikaula to da beach.

missing.usage: A chewy, sweet, glutinous rice cake that is a beloved dessert across Hawaii, appearing in variations like butter mochi, chi chi dango, and strawberry mochi.
examples: Aunty brought fresh butter mochi to da potluck.
Dis strawberry mochi stay broke da mouth.

missing.usage: A gift or offering given with aloha, often presented during celebrations, birthdays, or cultural ceremonies.
examples: I got one special makana for your birthday.
Mahalo for da beautiful makana!

missing.usage: An affectionate and respectful term for a grandfather or elderly male figure in the ohana.
examples: Tutu kane wen teach me how for throw net fishing.
My tutu kane get choke stories about old Hawaii.

missing.usage: An affectionate and respectful term for a grandmother or elderly matriarch in the family.
examples: Tutu wahine stay cooking in da kitchen.
We go visit tutu wahine this weekend.

missing.usage: A powerful, brave, capable woman who demonstrates strength, resilience, and leadership.
examples: She paddle through da rough surf like one true wahine toa.
Aunty is one wahine toa, she handle everything.

missing.usage: A phrase expressing profound appreciation, gratitude, and thankfulness.
examples: Mahalo nui loa for helping us fix da truck.

missing.usage: Encompassing the whole island from mountain ridge to shoreline; everywhere across land and sea.
examples: We wen search mauka makai for dat missing surfboard.
Da whole island stay celebrating mauka makai.
missing.origin: Hawaiian directional compound (mauka = mountain-ward, makai = ocean-ward)

missing.usage: Mackerel scad fish, highly prized in island waters as a staple food fish and premier live bait for big pelagic game fish.
examples: We wen catch one bucket of opelu off da ledge.
Crispy fried opelu with poi stay da best.

missing.usage: A friendly local slang term for a mixed-breed dog, or affectionately for someone of mixed heritage / multicultural background.
examples: My dog is one rescue poi dog, smart as anything.
He got one loyal poi dog dat follow him everywhere.

missing.usage: A large platter of mixed appetizers and finger foods served at parties, pau hana gatherings, and local diners.
examples: Order da pupu platter while we wait for da main food.

english: later you will learn the hard way
missing.usage: A classic local warning given to hardheaded or stubborn people meaning that consequences will eventually teach them a lesson.
examples: No touch dat hot pan! Bumbai you learn.
Go ahead, do silly tings, bumbai you learn.
missing.origin: Pidgin idiom (bumbai = by and by / later)

missing.usage: The essential Pidgin comparative meaning 'much better', 'superior', or 'way more enjoyable'.
examples: Going early morning is mo bettah, no get traffic.
Homemade poke stay mo bettah than store-bought.

missing.usage: A common loan phrase used in Hawaii conversation to tell someone to pause, slow down, or wait a second.
examples: Chotto matte brah, I still tying my shoes.
Chotto matte, lemme check da directions first.

english: Puerto Rican dance music in Hawaii
missing.usage: A lively genre of Puerto Rican dance music created by immigrants to Hawaii plantations, characterized by accordion, cuatro, and guiro rhythm.
examples: Dey playing kachi kachi music at da graduation party!
Everyone was dancing to da kachi kachi band.
missing.origin: Puerto Rican plantation culture in Hawaii

missing.usage: Originally sugarcane fiber waste; colloquially used in local plantation slang as a playful or biting term for a rascal or good-for-nothing.
examples: Dat guy acting like real bagasu.
Clean up all dat bagasu from da yard.

missing.usage: A button on clothing, or a button on an electronic switch/device.
examples: Push da botan for open da gate.
Your shirt missing one botan, brah.

missing.usage: Plantation-era slang word for breaking wind or flatulence.
examples: Who wen make totus in da car?!
Crack da window, someone wen make totus.

english: do not make a fool of yourself
missing.usage: Admonition instructing someone to behave with common sense and stop acting crazy or stupid.
examples: Behave in front da kumu, no make lolo.
No make lolo on camera, brah!

missing.usage: An emphatic slang descriptor meaning food that is so delicious it bursts with flavor (variant of 'broke da mouth').
examples: Aunty's ribs stay broke mouth ono!
Dat dessert was so broke mouth.

missing.usage: Severe highway or island road congestion where cars are packed tightly bumper-to-bumper.
examples: H-1 get choke traffic right now, take da back road.

missing.usage: A traditional beach necklace or jewelry item made from the worn, naturally holed tip of cone shells found along Hawaiian shorelines.
examples: He wearing his vintage puka shell necklace.

english: island greeting accompanied by shaka sign
missing.usage: The quintessential friendly Hawaii greeting and hand gesture expressing goodwill, friendliness, and solidarity.
examples: Shaka brah, good for see you!

english: make a fool of oneself in public
missing.usage: To humiliate or embarrass oneself in front of others by doing something clumsy, silly, or foolish.
examples: I slipped on da wet floor and wen make ass in front errbody.
